submission.natural_language_explanation: L4/H4 is a one-hot retrieve-and-copy head: at each position 0.5-1.0 of its attention sits on a single earlier token (0.87-1.00 in the scan's top examples, everything else under 0.1) and its OV circuit writes a soft copy of that token back into the residual stream (copying score +0.66), so the measured strength |W_O(z - mean z)| is a property of the retrieved token, not of the token at the peak: the same ' and' peak scores 1.20 when it retrieves ' nine' and 0.03 when it retrieves the opening 'The', and ' genus' scores 1.94 with ' Kl' retrieved but 1.04 with the continuation piece 'iella'. Retrieved tokens come in two kinds - the sink (the span's first token, or a punctuation that has just closed a sentence, often the current token itself at a period), whose write is 0.0-0.2 and which is what 56% of scanned tokens sit on and fall below the floor, or a content-word piece, typically the leading piece of a distinctive word (a name, place, number, code identifier or rare technical noun: ' Kl', ' Od', ' sp', ' K', ' China', ' b'), whose write is 0.6-2.3; the head leaves the sink only at a boundary position - a determiner, preposition, conjunction, comma, period or newline that follows such a word - and only when the query-key match falls in its sharply tuned, item-specific key set: in the fixed frames 'The committee met at ___ and read the minutes.' and 'The cat sat on the ___ and the dog slept by the door.' the sentence fires with ' nine', ' seven', ' six', ' mat', ' table', ' train' (0.8-1.5) and stays on the sink with ' noon', ' two', ' floor', ' door' (0.03-0.18). Predict active (0.6-2.3) for text of two or more clauses or sentences, or code that repeats a variable or identifier, that mentions such a piece and continues past it with a later boundary position; predict inactive (0.03-0.2) for a single short clause of once-used ordinary words (up to about 18 tokens), where the opening token and the closing period are the only retrieval targets.

rival_explanations: The head is a proper-name/entity tracker: it only leaves its sink for a capitalised name or a place, so ordinary concrete nouns such as ' mat', ' table', ' road', ' nine' or a repeated common noun should never carry it above the line, and only passages built around people or places should fire.

The head is a generic attention-mix unit whose write grows with how far the whole attention distribution is from its mean, so the peak is a function of text length and token diversity rather than of any particular retrieved word: any span of roughly twenty or more tokens should be active whatever it says, and swapping one word in a fourteen-token sentence should barely move it.

The head is an induction/duplicate n-gram head: it copies the token after an earlier copy of what it is currently reading, so it should fire on repeated or parallel text ('The dog ran across the field. The dog ran across the field.') and stay quiet on non-repetitive prose such as 'The spoliation case was based on the examination of a hard drive.' or 'Evgeniy Kljuykov published the genus Postiella in 1985.'.
